title: Contracts changed many times
question: Which construction contracts were modified most often, and do the documents say what staff could approve without a vote?
finding: 44 construction contracts show five or more modifications or change orders in the items on file, 20 of them ten or more. The most: Tutor Perini Corporation, Central Subway Project (1300) (Municipal Transportation Agency), 671. 6 of the 44 have an item that says in so many words what staff may approve without a further vote, such as an aggregate dollar amount the board set or a contingency the commission approved; the wording is in the last column. No document on disk publishes the individual change orders with their amounts, so whether changes were sized to stay under such a limit cannot be tested; the Budget and Legislative Analyst found the Public Utilities Commission keeps no central record of them for projects under $10 million.
how: The commissions that oversee construction (Public Utilities, Airport, Port, Public Works since late 2022, and the transit Board) vote on contract changes above what staff may approve, and on close-outs; those items were read into one record per contract number and department. The first figure is the original amount where an item prints it (or, for the Public Utilities Commission, the award in its minutes); otherwise it is the amount that stood before the first change on file, which already includes earlier staff-approved changes and so understates growth. The latest figure is the final amount at close-out, or the total in the latest item. Where the Board of Supervisors approved the same change as a commission, the commission's row is kept and the Board's dropped; where a numbered modification appears twice, the later row is kept. Design-build and construction-manager contracts, which grow as phases and work packages are added, and professional-services contracts are kept apart from fixed-price construction. The count for a contract is the highest modification number an item prints ("Modification No. 14 (Final)") or a count the item states ("modified 101 times", "671 change orders"), whichever is larger. The limit shown is the passage of an item that mentions 10% of the original contract, an approved contingency, or approval without a further vote, cut to 25 words. Dollars per modification is the rise over the first figure divided by that count.
limits: Amounts and days are copied from agenda items and minutes and parsed from their wording; contractor names are phrases from the item text. A total in an item is an authorization, often including contingency, not money paid. Most Public Works rows are agenda items as proposed, because minutes before 2025 are not posted. A contract appears in these files only when a change needed a commission vote, so small changes approved by staff are invisible, and departments set that line differently: rates can be compared within a department, not across. Change orders for conditions found underground and for work the owner adds are an ordinary part of construction. Many modifications are what a long project with thousands of line items produces, and a final modification often lowers the price to match the quantities actually built. A stated limit is delegated authority. The individual change orders, with dates and amounts, are in departments' construction-management systems and are what this screen would need.
